title: The chair: axial, equatorial, ring flips and substituents
goals: Use heats of formation per CH2 to rank rings by strain
Identify axial and equatorial positions on a chair and say what a ring flip does to them
Explain with a Newman projection why an axial group costs energy
Use the table of axial/equatorial energy differences to pick the more stable chair
Apply the three-step procedure: draw the chairs, compare their stability, state their relationship

sections.title: Table 5.1: heats of formation show that cyclohexane is the most stable ring
sections.html:
The lecture begins by putting numbers on the ring strain of the last lecture. The numbers are heats of formation, ΔH°f, in kcal/mol. A more negative heat of formation means a more stable compound. Rings of different sizes contain different numbers of atoms, so to compare them fairly the value is divided by the number of {{CH2}} groups.

Table 5.1, p. 198 (Jones and Fleming):

RingΔH°f (kcal/mol)ΔH°f per {{CH2}}
cyclopropane+12.7+4.2
cyclobutane+6.8+1.7
cyclopentane−18.7−3.7
cyclohexane (most stable)−29.5−4.9
cycloheptane−28.3−4.0
{{(CH2)}}∞, a strain-free chain−4.9

The last row is the reference: a {{CH2}} group in a very long open chain, where nothing is strained, contributes −4.9 kcal/mol. Read down the right-hand column against that reference. Cyclopropane and cyclobutane are far above it. Cyclopentane is close. Cyclohexane matches it exactly, which is the experimental proof that the chair has no angle strain and no torsional strain. Cycloheptane is slightly strained again, so the six-membered ring is the best of all.

micro.t: Turning the table into total ring strain
micro.h: The strain in each {{CH2}} is its value minus the strain-free value of −4.9. Multiply by the number of {{CH2}} groups to get the strain of the whole ring. Cyclopropane: (4.2 + 4.9) × 3 = about 27 kcal/mol. Cyclobutane: (1.7 + 4.9) × 4 = about 26 kcal/mol. Cyclopentane: (−3.7 + 4.9) × 5 = about 6 kcal/mol. Cyclohexane: (−4.9 + 4.9) × 6 = 0. Cycloheptane: (−4.0 + 4.9) × 7 = about 6 kcal/mol. The common mistake is to compare the left-hand column directly. Cycloheptane's −28.3 looks close to cyclohexane's −29.5, but it has one more {{CH2}} to share it among.

macro.t: Strain as a driving force on the past exam
macro.h: These numbers explain two mechanisms on the past exam. In Question 9 a four-membered ring expands to a five-membered ring: from the totals above, that releases roughly 20 kcal/mol of strain, which is why a ring bond migrates so readily. In Question 4B a three-membered epoxide ring is opened by methoxide, although an alkoxide is normally a poor leaving group: the ring holds about as much strain as cyclopropane. When a small ring opens or grows in a mechanism, relief of ring strain is usually the reason to write.

why.q: Why is the heat of formation divided by the number of CH2 groups before the rings are compared?
why.a: A larger ring has more bonds, so its total heat of formation is more negative simply because it is a bigger molecule. Dividing by the number of CH2 groups gives the energy of one CH2 in each ring, and that can be compared with a strain-free CH2 (−4.9 kcal/mol).

sections.title: Axial and equatorial: the two kinds of position on a chair
sections.html:
The lecture redraws the chair with its carbons numbered and names the two kinds of hydrogen.

[[chair:|A|H,num]]
  • The six vertical hydrogens are axial hydrogens. They point straight up or straight down, parallel to an axis through the middle of the ring.
  • The six hydrogens around the middle are equatorial hydrogens. They point outward, around the equator of the ring.

Three facts about these positions are used in every chair problem:

  1. Every carbon has one axial and one equatorial position.
  2. Axial positions alternate around the ring: up on carbon 1, down on carbon 2, up on carbon 3, and so on.
  3. On any one carbon, one of the two positions points to the top face of the ring and the other to the bottom face. Where the axial bond is up, the equatorial bond on that carbon slants slightly down, and the reverse.

So there are two independent descriptions of a position. Axial or equatorial says how the bond is oriented relative to the ring. Up or down says which face of the ring the group is on. Up and down decide cis and trans: two groups on the same face are cis, on opposite faces trans. Axial and equatorial decide energy, as the next sections show.

micro.t: Reading up or down for an equatorial group
micro.h: Axial groups are easy: the bond is vertical, so up or down is obvious. Equatorial bonds are nearly horizontal, and this is where mistakes happen. Use the axial bond on the same carbon as the guide. A carbon has only two positions outside the ring, and they point to opposite faces. So if the axial bond on that carbon points up, the equatorial group is the down group. If the axial bond points down, the equatorial group is the up group. Find the direction of the axial bond first, then take the opposite for the equatorial group.

macro.h: Question 4A of the past exam shows five chairs and asks cis or trans for each (50 points with the stability part). The trap is two equatorial groups on neighbouring carbons. They both seem to point sideways, so it is tempting to call them cis. Apply the rule in the closer look: on neighbouring carbons the axial bonds point in opposite directions, so one equatorial group is up and the other is down. Two equatorial groups on neighbouring carbons are trans. In the same way, a cis pair on carbons 1 and 2, or on carbons 1 and 4, always has one axial and one equatorial group.

why.q: Why is the equatorial position on a carbon down when the axial position on that carbon is up?
why.a: Each ring carbon is tetrahedral, with two bonds in the ring and two outside it. The two outside bonds point away from each other, to opposite faces of the ring. If one of them, the axial bond, is on the top face, the other one must be on the bottom face.

sections.title: The ring flip: K = 1, axial becomes equatorial, and no wedges on chairs
sections.html:
A chair is not rigid. It can turn into a second chair by a ring flip: the carbon at one end of the chair that points up swings down, and the carbon at the other end that points down swings up. No bond breaks. The flip happens by rotation about the C-C bonds.

To follow what happens to one position, mark a single hydrogen as D:

[[chair:1u:D|A]] [[chair:1u:D|B]]

The lecture records two facts about the flip:

  • For cyclohexane itself, K = 1. The two chairs have the same energy, so they are present in equal amounts.
  • After the flip, every axial H is equatorial and every equatorial H is axial.

What does not change is just as important. The labelled atom is up before the flip and up after it. A ring flip never changes up and down, so it never turns cis into trans. It changes only axial into equatorial.

The page ends with a drawing rule in the professor's words: “No wedges or dashed wedges when drawing chairs.” Wedges and dashes belong on the flat hexagon, where they are the only way to show up and down. A chair is already a three-dimensional picture, and the direction of each bond shows where the group is.

micro.h:
The ring cannot go from one chair to the other without passing through strained shapes on the way. The highest point is a half-chair, about 10.8 kcal/mol above the chair. In the middle of the path is a shallow valley, the twist-boat, about 5.5 kcal/mol above the chair.

[[energy:R=0,TS1=10.8,I=5.5,TS2=10.8,P=0|I=twist-boat]]

A barrier of about 11 kcal/mol is small. At room temperature a cyclohexane ring flips roughly a hundred thousand times each second. So the two chairs cannot be separated or put in separate bottles. They are two conformations of one compound, in equilibrium, and the question to ask is which one the molecule spends more time in.

micro.t: Why wedges on a chair lose points
micro.h: On a flat hexagon a wedge means toward you, which is up, and a dash means away, which is down. On a chair, up is drawn as a bond that actually points up the page, or slants up for an equatorial bond. Adding a wedge to a chair bond gives the reader two signals that can disagree, and a grader has no way to know which one you meant. When you convert a flat drawing to a chair, read each wedge as up and each dash as down, place the group in the up or down position on its carbon, and then leave the wedges behind.

macro.t: Every chair question needs both chairs
macro.h: Because the flip is fast, any property of a cyclohexane depends on both chairs. Question 8 of the past exam asks for both chairs of three molecules. Question 5B needs the flipped chair of a hexachlorocyclohexane to show that neither chair has a hydrogen anti to a chlorine. Question 3D needs the chair in which the leaving group is axial, even though it is the less stable one, because E2 happens from that chair. The habit to build: draw one chair, flip it, and move every group from axial to equatorial or back while keeping it up or down.

why.q: A ring flip turns every axial group equatorial. Why can it not turn a cis compound into a trans compound?
why.a: The flip only rotates about C-C bonds, and no bond is broken. Each group stays on the same face of the ring, up or down, that it started on. Cis and trans are defined by faces, so they survive the flip. Changing cis to trans would need a bond to break.

sections.title: Methylcyclohexane: the equatorial chair wins, K = 19.5
sections.html:
Put one methyl group on the ring and the two chairs are no longer equal. The lecture starts from the flat drawing with {{CH3}} on a wedge:

[[ring:1u:CH3]]

The wedge says the methyl is up. It does not say axial or equatorial, because that depends on the chair. In one chair the up position on carbon 1 is axial. After the ring flip the same up position is equatorial.

[[chair:1u:CH3|A]] [[chair:1u:CH3|B]]

The lecture's labels and numbers:

ChairEnergy
{{CH3}} axialhigher energy
{{CH3}} equatoriallower energy

For the equilibrium written from axial to equatorial, K = 19.5 and the energy difference is {{dG}} = 1.74 kcal/mol in favour of the equatorial chair.

The sentence to carry through the rest of the unit is the one the professor wrote under the chairs: “Axial groups cost energy.” At any instant about 19 or 20 molecules have the methyl equatorial for each one that has it axial. Both chairs exist, and they interconvert constantly, but the molecule spends most of its time in the equatorial one.

micro.t: From K to a percentage, and from K to ΔG
micro.h: K = 19.5 means 19.5 equatorial molecules for every 1 axial molecule. The fraction equatorial is 19.5 / (19.5 + 1) = 0.95, so about 95% equatorial and 5% axial. A common mistake is to say that the axial chair does not exist. It does: one molecule in twenty. To connect K and energy, use {{dG}} = −RT ln K with RT = 0.592 kcal/mol at 25 °C. The size of the difference is 0.592 × ln 19.5 = 0.592 × 2.97 = 1.76 kcal/mol, which agrees with the table's 1.74 within rounding. The sign is negative for axial going to equatorial: that direction is downhill.

macro.h: The rule that groups prefer equatorial positions is why glucose is the most common sugar in nature. In the chair of β-D-glucose every substituent on the ring, the four OH groups and the {{CH2OH}} group, is equatorial. No other sugar of its family can do that. On the past exam the preference is tested directly: Question 4A asks whether each drawn chair is the most stable conformation, and Question 8 asks you to circle the more stable of two chairs. Both come down to asking which groups are axial and what that costs.

why.q: The flat drawing shows the methyl on a wedge. Why does that not tell you whether the methyl is axial or equatorial?
why.a: A wedge fixes only the face of the ring: the methyl is up. On a given carbon the up position is axial in one chair and equatorial in the other, and the two chairs interconvert. So the wedge is true of both chairs, and the molecule chooses the equatorial one because it is lower in energy.

sections.title: Why axial costs energy: two gauche interactions with the ring
sections.html:
The lecture explains the 1.74 kcal/mol with a Newman projection looking down the C2-C1 bond. C2 is the front carbon and C1, which carries the methyl, is the back carbon. On the front carbon, the ring continues to C3. On the back carbon, the ring continues to C6.

With the methyl axial:

[[newman:C3,H,H|CH3,H,C6|60]]

The axial {{CH3}} is 60° away from the ring carbon C3. That is a gauche interaction, the same one found in gauche butane, where two {{CH3}} groups are 60° apart:

[[newman:CH3,H,H|CH3,H,H|60]]

With the methyl equatorial:

[[newman:C3,H,H|H,CH3,C6|60]]

Now the {{CH3}} is 180° from C3. It is anti to the ring carbon: no gauche interaction, just as in anti butane:

[[newman:CH3,H,H|H,CH3,H|60]]

The axial methyl has a second gauche interaction on its other side, which the professor left as homework: look down the C6-C1 bond and the axial {{CH3}} is gauche to C5. The summary line in the notes:

Groups in axial position: 2 gauche interactions with the ring.

An equatorial group has none, because it is anti to both C3 and C5.

micro.h: One gauche interaction between two carbon groups in butane costs about 0.9 kcal/mol. An axial methyl has two of them with the ring, and 2 × 0.87 = 1.74 kcal/mol, the value in the lecture. So the axial penalty is the gauche butane number counted twice. This is a useful check on any chair problem that involves methyl groups: count the gauche interactions between carbon groups in each chair, multiply by about 0.9 kcal/mol, and compare the totals.

micro.t: The same thing under another name: 1,3-diaxial
micro.h: Many books describe the axial penalty as 1,3-diaxial interactions. An axial methyl on C1 points the same way as the axial hydrogens on C3 and C5, and it bumps into them. This is not a different effect. The carbon that is gauche to the methyl (C3, then C5) is the carbon that holds the axial hydrogen the methyl bumps into. Two gauche interactions with the ring and two 1,3-diaxial interactions are two descriptions of one crowding. Use the lecture's wording, gauche interactions, when you explain it on the exam.

macro.t: An old idea reused, and a price that E2 has to pay
macro.h: Nothing new was needed to explain the chair: the gauche and anti conformations of butane already contain the answer. That is typical of this course, where a small set of ideas keeps returning. The cost of an axial group also matters for reactions. An E2 elimination on a cyclohexane needs the leaving group to be axial, with an axial hydrogen on the next carbon. In Question 3D of the past exam the reacting chair has both Cl and {{CH3}} axial. That chair is the less stable one, but it is the only one that can react.

why.q: Why does an equatorial methyl group have no gauche interactions with the ring?
why.a: An equatorial bond points away from the ring. Seen down the C2-C1 bond, the equatorial methyl is 180° from C3, and seen down the C6-C1 bond it is 180° from C5. It is anti to both ring carbons, like the two methyl groups of anti butane, so there is no crowding to pay for.

sections.title: Table 5.3: how much each group prefers the equatorial position
sections.html:
Different groups pay different prices for being axial. Table 5.3, p. 207 lists the difference in energy of the chair conformations, axial against equatorial, and the equilibrium constant that goes with it:

Group{{dG}} axial/equatorial (kcal/mol){{Keq}}
methyl1.7419.5
ethyl1.7921.2
propyl2.2143.4
1-methylethyl (isopropyl)2.6186.0
1,1-dimethylethyl (tert-butyl)5.511,916

How to use the table:

  • A bigger number means a bigger group, in the sense that matters on a ring. When two groups compete for the one equatorial position, the group with the larger value gets it.
  • Methyl and ethyl are almost the same: 1.74 and 1.79. Isopropyl is clearly larger. tert-Butyl is in a class of its own.
  • With {{Keq}} = 11,916, a tert-butyl group is equatorial in more than 99.99% of the molecules. For practical purposes it locks the ring in one chair.

These are the lecture's values and the ones the exam expects. Other tables give somewhat smaller numbers for some groups (ethyl about 1.75, propyl about 1.8, isopropyl about 2.1 to 2.2). Use 1.79, 2.21 and 2.61 here.

micro.t: Why ethyl is barely bigger than methyl, and tert-butyl is huge
micro.h: The axial penalty comes from crowding against the ring. An axial ethyl group can rotate about its bond to the ring so that its extra {{CH3}} points away from the ring and only hydrogens point in. Seen from the ring it looks almost like a methyl group, which is why 1.79 is so close to 1.74. An isopropyl group can still turn its single hydrogen inward, though with fewer comfortable rotations available. A tert-butyl group has three {{CH3}} groups on the attached carbon. However it rotates, one {{CH3}} points into the ring toward the axial hydrogens, and the crowding is severe: 5.5 kcal/mol.

The two columns are linked by {{dG}} = RT ln K for the size of the difference, with RT = 0.592 kcal/mol at 25 °C. Isopropyl: 0.592 × ln 86.0 = 0.592 × 4.45 = 2.64, against 2.61 in the table. tert-Butyl: 0.592 × ln 11,916 = 0.592 × 9.39 = 5.56, against 5.5. The agreement is within about 1%, which is rounding and a slightly different temperature. Going the other way, K = e raised to the power ({{dG}} / RT). Each additional 1.36 kcal/mol multiplies K by 10, which is a handy number for estimates.

macro.h: Question 8, part i, of the past exam is cis-1-ethyl-2-methylcyclohexane. One chair has ethyl equatorial and methyl axial, the other the reverse. The table says ethyl is larger, 1.79 against 1.74, so the chair with ethyl equatorial is more stable, but only slightly. In Question 4A, chair 2 has an axial isopropyl and an equatorial OH, so it is not the most stable: flip it. In part ii of Question 8 one chair has both groups equatorial and the other has both axial, and the costs add: about 1.74 + 2.61 = 4.35 kcal/mol against the diaxial chair.

why.q: Why is the tert-butyl value (5.5) so much larger than the isopropyl value (2.61), when the group has only one more carbon?
why.a: An axial isopropyl group can rotate so that its one hydrogen points toward the ring. A tert-butyl group has no hydrogen on the attached carbon, so one of its three methyl groups always points into the ring and collides with the axial hydrogens. The crowding cannot be avoided by rotation, so the cost is much higher.

sections.title: The three-step procedure for any substituted cyclohexane
sections.html:
Under Table 5.3 the professor wrote the procedure for every chair question:

  1. Draw chairs. Both of them.
  2. Determine which, if any, is more stable.
  3. Compare chairs → relationship: same? diastereomers? enantiomers?

Work it once on cis-1-ethyl-2-methylcyclohexane, both groups on wedges:

[[ring:1u:CH3,2u:CH2CH3]]

Step 1. Both groups are up. On neighbouring carbons, one up position is axial and the other is equatorial. Draw one chair, then flip it: each group changes between axial and equatorial and stays up.

[[chair:1u:CH3,2u:CH2CH3|A]] [[chair:1u:CH3,2u:CH2CH3|B]]

Step 2. The first chair has methyl axial (cost 1.74) and ethyl equatorial. The second has ethyl axial (cost 1.79). The first chair, with the larger group equatorial, is more stable, by a small margin.

Step 3. The chairs have different energies, so they cannot be the same and cannot be mirror images. They are diastereomers.

RelationshipTestExample
samethe chairs can be superimposedcis-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane
enantiomersnon-superimposable mirror images, equal energycis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane
diastereomersneither of the above, usually different energymethylcyclohexane

The words in the notes, “which, if any”, are a reminder that sometimes neither chair is more stable.

micro.h: Two structures that are identical have the same energy. Two enantiomers also have the same energy, because a mirror does not change any distance inside a molecule. So if step 2 finds that the two chairs have different energies, the relationship must be diastereomers, and step 3 is finished. Only when the two chairs have equal energy is there a real choice between same and enantiomers. To decide, draw the mirror image of chair 1 and see whether chair 2 matches it, or try to turn chair 2 in space until it lies on chair 1. The next section does this for cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane.

Number the carbons on the flat drawing and on both chairs, in the same direction. Mark each group u or d from its wedge or dash. In the first chair, put each group in the up or down position of its carbon, and read whether that position is axial or equatorial. For the second chair do not rethink anything: every group keeps its u or d and swaps axial for equatorial. Then check that the second chair agrees with the flat drawing. Most lost points in chair questions come from a group that changed face during the flip.

macro.t: Question 8 is this procedure three times
macro.h: Question 8 of the past exam is worth 100 points and is exactly these three steps for three molecules: cis-1-ethyl-2-methylcyclohexane (ethyl equatorial is more stable, diastereomers), trans-1-isopropyl-4-methylcyclohexane (both equatorial is more stable, diastereomers) and cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane (equal energy, enantiomers). The answer for each part has three pieces, one per step, and each piece earns points. Writing the three steps as headings on the exam page makes it hard to forget one, and the relationship is the piece most often left out.

why.q: Why must two chairs with different energies be diastereomers?
why.a: Identical structures have identical energies, and so do enantiomers, since mirror images contain the same distances and interactions. If two chairs of the same molecule differ in energy they are neither identical nor mirror images. Stereoisomers that are not mirror images are diastereomers.

sections.title: cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane: two chairs of equal energy that are mirror images
sections.html:
The last page applies the procedure to cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane. In the flat drawing both methyls are on wedges, and the notes mark the molecule achiral: the flat drawing has a mirror plane that passes between C1 and C2.

[[ring:1u:CH3,2u:CH3]]

Step 1: draw chairs.

[[chair:1u:CH3,2u:CH3|A]] [[chair:1u:CH3,2u:CH3|B]]
C1 {{CH3}}C2 {{CH3}}
Chair 1axial (up)equatorial (up)
Chair 2, after the ring flipequatorial (up)axial (up)

Step 2: which is more stable? Neither. Each chair has one axial methyl and one equatorial methyl, so the ring flip has K = 1: the chairs have the same energy.

Step 3: relationship. Equal energy leaves two possibilities, same or enantiomers. The lecture settles it by drawing chair 1 next to its mirror image: the mirror image is the flipped chair, and it cannot be superimposed on chair 1. In the professor's words, “these chair conformations are non-superimposable mirror images.” The two chairs are conformational enantiomers.

So each chair, frozen, is chiral, but the compound is achiral: the two mirror-image chairs interconvert rapidly and are always present in exactly equal amounts.

micro.t: Counting gauche interactions shows why K is exactly 1
micro.h: In chair 1 the axial methyl on C1 has two gauche interactions with the ring. The equatorial methyl on C2 has none with the ring. The two methyl groups, on neighbouring carbons with one axial and one equatorial, are 60° apart, which is one more gauche interaction. Total: three, or about 3 × 0.87 = 2.6 kcal/mol of strain. In chair 2 the roles of C1 and C2 are exchanged and the count is again three. The strain does not disappear, but it is identical in the two chairs, so {{dG}} = 0 and K = 1.

It can seem contradictory that a molecule is achiral while every chair of it is chiral. The resolution is time. A sample would be optically active only if one enantiomer were in excess. Here each molecule turns into its own mirror image about a hundred thousand times per second by ring flipping, so the sample is always an exact 50:50 mixture and nothing can be separated. The flat drawing, with its mirror plane, represents this average correctly. For deciding whether a cyclohexane is chiral, use the flat drawing. For energy and for reactions, use the chairs.

macro.t: This exact molecule is Question 8, part iii
macro.h: The past exam asks for both chairs of cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, the more stable one, and the relationship. The full-credit answer is the one from this lecture: one axial and one equatorial methyl in each chair, equal in energy, and the chairs are enantiomers (non-superimposable mirror images). The usual wrong answers are to circle one chair as more stable, or to call the chairs the same because they have the same energy. Compare the trans isomer, where one chair has both methyls equatorial and the other has both axial: different energies, so diastereomers.

why.q: Why is K exactly 1 for the ring flip of cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, when K is 19.5 for methylcyclohexane?
why.a: In methylcyclohexane the flip moves the only methyl from axial to equatorial, which removes two gauche interactions. In the cis-1,2 compound the flip moves one methyl out of the axial position and the other into it. Each chair has the same set of interactions, so their energies are equal and neither is favoured.

homework.q: HW: find the other gauche interaction and draw a Newman projection to show it.

steps.h: The lecture looked down the C2-C1 bond of axial methylcyclohexane. C1 carries the axial {{CH3}}. From the front carbon, C2, the ring continues to C3, and the axial {{CH3}} is 60° from C3: gauche.

steps.t: Find the other bond to look down
steps.h: C1 has two ring bonds, one to C2 and one to C6. The ring is the same on both sides of C1, so the second interaction must be found by looking down the other ring bond, C6-C1. Put C6 in front and C1 behind.

steps.t: List the groups on each carbon
steps.h: Front carbon C6: the ring bond to C5 and two hydrogens. Back carbon C1: the axial {{CH3}}, one hydrogen (the equatorial one) and the ring bond to C2.

Place C5 at the top of the front carbon. On the back carbon, the ring bond to C2 is 60° to one side of C5 (the ring carbons are gauche to each other in a chair), the axial {{CH3}} is 60° to the other side of C5, and the hydrogen is opposite C5.
[[newman:C5,H,H|C2,H,CH3|60]]
The axial {{CH3}} is 60° from C5: a second gauche interaction, the mirror image of the first. With the methyl equatorial, the {{CH3}} and the H on C1 change places and the {{CH3}} is anti to C5.

homework.answer: Look down the C6-C1 bond. The axial CH3 on C1 is gauche (60°) to C5. Together with the interaction with C3 seen down C2-C1, an axial group has 2 gauche interactions with the ring, about 2 × 0.87 = 1.74 kcal/mol for methyl.

summary: Heats of formation per CH2 show that cyclohexane (−4.9 kcal/mol, the same as a strain-free chain) is the most stable ring.
A chair has six axial positions, vertical and alternating up and down, and six equatorial positions around the middle.
A ring flip turns every axial position equatorial and every equatorial position axial, but never changes up and down, so cis stays cis.
Chairs are drawn without wedges or dashes.
Axial groups cost energy: for methyl, K = 19.5 and ΔG = 1.74 kcal/mol in favour of equatorial, because an axial group has 2 gauche interactions with the ring.
The cost grows with the group: methyl 1.74, ethyl 1.79, propyl 2.21, isopropyl 2.61, tert-butyl 5.5 kcal/mol, and the larger group takes the equatorial position.
For any substituted cyclohexane: draw the chairs, decide which if any is more stable, then state the relationship (same, enantiomers or diastereomers).
The two chairs of cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane have equal energy (K = 1) and are conformational enantiomers.
